title: Following the Crowd: How Two Hunches Can Steer Millions

source.title: A Theory of Fads, Fashion, Custom, and Cultural Change as Informational Cascades
source.authors: Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer, and Ivo Welch

intro.summary: Why do people copy each other so readily, and why do crowd behaviours like fads, medical fashions and bank runs sometimes flip suddenly? Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992) model people who decide in a line. Each sees only earlier choices plus one private clue, and they show that sensible people soon ignore their own clue (an 'informational cascade'). Such cascades are often wrong, rest on very little information, and can be shattered by one small piece of public news. Hisakado and Mori (2015) extend a simpler 'herder' version of the idea to networks: they find that hubs (highly connected people) do not change the herder share at which a crowd can lock onto the wrong answer, though hubs do change how fast votes settle. Main limits and open questions: both are mathematical models with strong simplifications (identical clues, fixed order, mean-field approximations, a 50% copying threshold), the field evidence is suggestive rather than causal, and the two papers model followers differently (rational inference versus a mechanical majority rule); good follow-ups are lab tests such as Anderson and Holt's urn experiment, cascades on small-world networks, and reputational cascades.
background: A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. A conditional probability is how likely something is once you know some other fact, such as the chance a restaurant is good given that it is busy.
Bayesian updating means starting with a belief and shifting it by the right amount each time a new clue arrives.
A network is a set of people (nodes) joined by links. A 'hub' is someone with far more links than most.
Herd behaviour means many people doing the same thing. An informational cascade is one specific reason for it: copying because others' choices seem to carry information.
intro.aha: A cascade followed by millions of people may rest on just one or two people's private hunches, so a single public clue weaker than one person's hunch can reverse the whole crowd.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: People copy each other everywhere: in fashion, medicine, investing, and which restaurant to try. Copying is often sensible, yet crowds also get things badly wrong and then suddenly change course. The authors ask one question. Can a single, rational reason for copying explain both why crowds agree so quickly and why that agreement is so easy to break?
primer.quote: An informational cascade occurs when it is optimal for an individual, having observed the actions of those ahead of him, to follow the behavior of the preceding individual without regard to his own information.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They built a simple model. People stand in a line and each decides whether to adopt something, like a new seed or a treatment. Each person gets one private clue that is right more often than not. Each person also sees what everyone ahead chose, but not the clues behind those choices. Later work by Hisakado and Mori put a simpler 'herder' version on networks, where each voter looks at only a few earlier voters, sometimes chosen through popular hubs.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: After just two people lean the same way, the third person should copy them whatever her own clue says. From then on, every later choice is a copy, so it adds no new information. Crowds therefore lock in fast and on little evidence, and they often lock onto the wrong answer. Because a huge crowd may rest on only one or two real clues, a small public announcement can tip it over.
primer.quote: The release of a small amount of public information can shatter a long-lasting cascade, where a "small amount" refers to a signal less informative than the private signal of a single individual.

primer.heading: What happens on networks
primer.body: Hisakado and Mori found that once the share of copiers ('herders') passes a tipping point, a vote can settle on either the right or the wrong answer. Adding influential hubs did not move that tipping point. Hubs only changed how quickly the vote settled. Their results rest on approximations and computer simulations, and they assume herders simply follow the majority of the few voters they see.
primer.quote: In conclusion, the influence of hubs can only be seen in the convergence speed and cannot be seen in the phase transition between the one-peak and two-peaks phases.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: If crowds rest on thin evidence, then 'everyone is doing it' is weak proof. Fresh, independent evidence is always worth gathering. This is why some military courts let the lowest rank vote first and some countries ban polls just before elections. These are models, though. Real people also copy out of social pressure, reputation or a wish to fit in, and the real-world examples are suggestive, not proof that cascades caused them.
primer.quote: Thus the fact that a vast segment of society already smokes need not discourage investigation of the effects of smoking.

concepts.title: One private clue nudges your belief
concepts.idea: A clue that is right more often than not should shift your belief toward what it points to, by an amount set by how accurate the clue is.

predict.question: A new case: one friend's restaurant tips turn out right only 40% of the time, so she is wrong more often than right. You start 50–50 about a new place, and she says it is good. Where should your belief that it is good end up?
options: It rises a little, because any 'good' tip is some good news
It stays at 50%, because a clue this unreliable tells you nothing
It falls to about 40%, because her 'good' points the wrong way more often than not
It rises to about 60%, because she is right 40% of the time
why: It is tempting to treat any 'good' word as good news. But a clue only pushes you toward what it says when it is right more than half the time. Below half, it pushes the other way.
Only a clue right exactly half the time (a coin flip) leaves you unmoved. A clue right 40% of the time is wrong 60% of the time, and that pattern is itself information.
Correct. From 50–50, the after-belief equals how often the 'good' clue is right when the place is good. Here that is 40%. Her tip is useful, but read in reverse.
This mixes up 40% and 60%. She says 'good' and is wrong 60% of the time, so 'good' points away from good, not toward it.

terms.means: A clue only you see, such as the ball you drew from an urn or your own first taste of the food
How often that kind of clue points to the right answer
How likely you thought something was before the new clue arrived
Your updated belief after taking the clue into account

model.title: Your belief that the restaurant is good, before and after one clue
model.note: Teaching model: one person, one yes-or-no question (is it good?), and one clue whose accuracy is known exactly and is the same whether the place is good or bad. This is the Bayes'-rule step taken by the very first person in the basic cascade model (Wikipedia's 'Quantitative description' of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch, 1992). Real people may not know how accurate a clue is, and the model leaves that out. Numbers are illustrative, not data from either source.

Then a clue arrives, like a friend's tip. This switch sets whether the clue says 'good' or 'bad'.
This slider sets how often this kind of clue turns out right. Watch the right bar move.
This slider sets how sure you were to begin with.
The right bar is your belief after the clue, and this box shows how far it moved.

explore.prompt: Play with how good the clue is and where you start. Can you make a clue that hardly matters, and one that changes your mind?

goals.text: Starting from 50–50, make a 'good' clue that still nudges you the right way but moves you by no more than 6 points.
hints: Keep your starting belief at 50–50, with the clue saying 'good'.
From a 50–50 start, the after bar lands on the clue's accuracy.
You want a clue only slightly better than a coin flip, but not a coin flip itself.

goals.text: Start fairly sure the place is bad, with only a 20% belief that it's good. Then find a 'good' clue accurate enough to tip you past 50%.
hints: First set your starting belief to 20%, with the clue saying 'good'.
A doubtful start needs a much more accurate clue to cross the middle line.
Raise accuracy one notch at a time. A clue right four times out of five only brings you to a dead tie.

feedback.correct: Right. A clue moves you toward what it says only if it is right more than half the time. Her 'good' is right just 40% of the time, so from 50–50 it should pull you down to 40%.
feedback.incorrect: The size and direction of the push both come from how often the clue is right. At exactly 50% it is noise and moves nothing. Above 50% it pushes toward what it says. Below 50% it pushes the other way. From a 50–50 start you land on 40%.

steps.say: Start at 50–50 with a clue that is right only half the time, which is no better than a coin flip. The after bar does not budge. A clue that is no better than chance tells you nothing.
Now make the clue right 60% of the time. A 'good' clue lifts you to 60%. A clue that only you get to see is called a private signal.
Make it right 90% of the time and the bar jumps to 90%. How far you move depends on how often the clue is right, its signal accuracy.
Flip the clue to 'bad'. The accuracy is the same, so the push is the same size, but in the opposite direction: you drop to 10%.
Now start doubtful. Your prior belief, your belief before the clue, is 20%. A 70%-accurate 'good' clue lifts you to only about 37%. You still lean towards 'bad'.
Start hopeful at 80%, and the same clue lifts you to about 90%. Your posterior belief, where you end up, blends where you started with what the clue says.
Last, a strong doubt meets a strong clue. A 5% hunch plus a 95%-accurate 'good' clue lands exactly on 50%. One clue nudges your belief. It does not override everything you already believed.

understand.explanation: A clue that is right more often than not should move your belief toward what it says. How far it moves you depends on two things: how accurate the clue is, and where you started. A clue right exactly half the time is noise and moves nothing. From a 50–50 start, you land on the clue's accuracy. In Anderson's urn experiment, urn A holds two 'a' balls and one 'b', so drawing an 'a' should take a 50–50 guesser to about 67% for urn A. In the basic cascade model of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992), the first person in line has nothing but this one clue, so 'the first individual adopts if his signal is H and rejects if it is L'. Wikipedia shows this step with Bayes' rule. The model assumes people know exactly how accurate their clue is and update perfectly. That is a simplifying assumption, not an observed fact about real people.
understand.quote: The equation says that, by virtue of the fact that q > 0.5, the first agent, acting only on his private signal, will always increase his estimate of p with an H signal.

connect.caption: This is Wikipedia's Bayes'-rule equation for the first person. A means 'accepting is right' (the place is good), H means the clue says 'good', p is your starting belief and q is how often the clue is right. The result is your after-belief. When the clue says 'bad', the model swaps q and 1 − q. Watch the notation: the 1992 paper uses p for the clue's accuracy and fixes the starting belief at 1/2.

concepts.recap: One clue moves you toward what it says. How far depends on how accurate the clue is and on how sure you were already. A coin-flip clue moves you not at all.

concepts.title: When two earlier choices outvote your own clue
concepts.idea: Once the choices you can read as clues lead by two in one direction, your single private clue can no longer change your best decision, so you copy: a cascade begins.

predict.question: A new person reaches the restaurant. Ahead of her, in order, one person walked away, then two went in. Her own clue says 'bad'. Her starting belief is 50–50, and everyone's clue is equally reliable. What is her best choice?
options: Go in: the last two people in a row went in
She is exactly torn, so either choice is equally good (the model flips a coin)
Walk away: her own clue says bad, and she should trust it
Go in: three people have already decided, so she is surely in a cascade
why: A run of two in a row feels decisive, but what counts is the net lead. One walk-away and two go-ins is a lead of only one, not two.

Correct. The lead is one toward going in, and her 'bad' clue cancels it exactly. Her belief is back at 50%, and the paper's tie rule is to flip a coin. She is in the same spot as the second person in the queue.
Her clue does count, but here it only balances the lead of one. It does not tip her toward walking away. Her belief lands at exactly 50%.
The number of people ahead does not matter. Only the lead does. One walk-away cancels one go-in, so the lead is one and her clue still matters.

terms.means: The point where a person's best choice no longer depends on their own clue, so they copy the choices ahead of them, and everyone after them does the same
A cascade in which everyone goes in (adopts), whatever their own clues say
A cascade in which everyone walks away (rejects), whatever their own clues say

model.title: Your belief that the restaurant is good, after a queue of earlier choices and your own clue
model.note: Teaching model: one yes-or-no question (is the new restaurant good?). Everyone's clue is equally reliable, everyone sees every earlier choice, and the restaurant is equally good or bad for all. Each earlier choice in the lead is counted as revealing exactly one clue, as in the basic model of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992, Section II.A). There is one subtlety this leaves out. In the paper, a person who is exactly torn flips a coin, so their choice can be weaker evidence than a clue. The paper shows that two ahead still makes the third person copy. A lead of three cannot actually come from people who all followed their own clues when the start is 50–50; it is here only so you can explore. You go in when your belief is above 50%, walk away below it, and flip a coin at exactly 50%. Numbers are illustrative, not data from either source.

controls.label: How often this kind of clue is right
Your belief it's good, before the clue
Lead of earlier choices: went in minus walked away

outputs.label: Belief from earlier choices only
outputs.expr: p * pow(q, lead) / (p * pow(q, lead) + (1 - p) * pow(1 - q, lead))

outputs.label: Belief after your own clue too
outputs.expr: p * pow(q, lead + (up ? 1 : -1)) / (p * pow(q, lead + (up ? 1 : -1)) + (1 - p) * pow(1 - q, lead + (up ? 1 : -1)))

outputs.label: Chance you go in if your clue says good
Chance you go in if your clue says bad
How much flipping your clue changes your choice

steps.say: Same picture as before: your belief that the new restaurant is good. Now there's a queue of people ahead of you, and a new middle bar shows what their choices alone suggest.
This new slider is the lead: how many more people ahead went in than walked away. Here, one more went in.
Two new readouts: your chance of going in, and how much flipping your own clue changes that choice.

explore.prompt: Flip your own clue back and forth at different leads. Watch when it stops mattering, and whether a sharper clue can save it.

goals.text: Keep the starting belief at 50%. Find the smallest lead toward going in at which flipping your own clue no longer changes what you do.
hints: Your clue matters as long as flipping it changes your chance of going in.
Step the lead up one at a time, and flip your clue at each step. Watch 'How much flipping your clue changes your choice'.
At one lead, flipping still turns a sure 'go in' into a coin flip. Go one step further.

goals.text: Show that a very reliable clue still gets outvoted. Keep the 50% start, make clues right nearly all the time, then make a 'bad' clue lose to the earlier choices using as small a lead as possible.
hints: Which slider sets how reliable the clues are? It sets theirs as well as yours.
Push clue reliability up, switch your clue to 'bad', then try small leads toward going in.
A sharper clue makes each earlier choice more convincing too, so the lead you need doesn't grow.

feedback.correct: Right. What matters is the net lead of choices you can read as clues, not the order or a recent streak. A lead of one, met by an opposite clue, leaves her exactly at 50%, torn between the two.
feedback.incorrect: The pull to follow a streak, or to count heads, is natural. But each earlier choice counts as one clue for or against. One walk-away cancels one go-in, so the lead is just one, and her 'bad' clue cancels that, which leaves her at 50%.

steps.say: Nobody ahead of you yet: the lead is zero. Your clue says good, so your belief rises to 60% and you go in.
Flip your clue to 'bad': 40%, so you walk away. Here your clue decides everything. Flipping it swings your choice by 100 points.
Now one person ahead went in. You can read that choice as their clue: they probably saw 'good'. Their choice alone puts you at 60%, and your own 'good' clue lifts you to about 69%.
But if your clue says 'bad', it cancels theirs exactly: 50%. You're torn, so you flip a coin. Your clue still matters, but only half as much: the swing is 50 points.
Two more people went in than walked away. Their choices alone put you near 69%. Your 'bad' clue pulls you down only to 60%, which is still above half, so you go in anyway.
Flip your clue to 'good': about 77%. You go in either way. The swing is zero. Your own clue no longer changes what you do.
This is an information cascade: two clues ahead outweigh your one, so you copy. Your choice now ignores your clue, so the next person learns nothing new from it and copies too.
When everyone goes in like this, it's an up cascade. A lead of two toward walking away would start a down cascade, the same thing in the other direction.

understand.explanation: Each earlier choice is a clue you can read: someone who went in probably had a 'good' clue. When everyone's clue is equally reliable, your belief just counts clues, goods minus bads. With a lead of two, your one clue can at most cut that to one, which is still in favour, so you copy whatever your clue says. This is an information cascade: an up cascade if everyone goes in, a down cascade if everyone walks away. Copying here is a sensible reading of the evidence, not peer pressure, and because your choice now reveals nothing about your clue, the next person faces the same lead and copies too. Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992) worked this out step by step for the first three people in their basic model and proved that, under mild assumptions, a cascade almost surely starts as the queue grows. These are theoretical results with strong assumptions (equally reliable clues, every earlier choice visible); in Anderson and Holt's urn experiment, as reported on Wikipedia, cascades appeared in 41 of 56 runs, so real people often but not always behave this way.
understand.quote: The third individual is faced with one of three situations: (1) both predecessors have adopted (in which case even an L signal induces him to adopt and thus creates an up cascade)

check.task: Keep the starting belief at 50%. Put the model in a state where your own clue says 'good', yet your best choice is certainly to walk away.
check.hint: Earlier choices can lead in either direction. The lead slider goes below zero.
check.misconception: A sensible person always follows their own evidence, so going against your own clue must be a mistake. In fact, when the choices ahead outweigh your single clue, ignoring it is the best use of all the evidence you have.

connect.caption: Wikipedia's Bayes'-rule update for the n-th person. p is your starting belief and q is how often a clue is right, as on the sliders. a counts 'went in' choices plus your clue if good; b counts 'walked away' choices plus your clue if bad. Only a − b matters: the lead plus or minus one for your clue. The original paper (s2) writes clue accuracy as p, so watch the letters.

concepts.recap: When the choices ahead lead by two, your one clue can't change your best choice, so you copy, and a cascade begins.

concepts.title: Cascades start fast and are often wrong
concepts.idea: Because a cascade locks in after only a few clues, the chance it locks onto the wrong choice stays surprisingly high even when each person's clue is quite accurate.

predict.question: A town's clues are each right 75% of the time. The line of people choosing one after another grows from 10 people to 1,000. What happens to the chance the town ends up all copying the wrong choice?
options: It falls close to zero, because 1,000 clues are plenty to find the truth
It barely changes and stays near 19%, because the first few people already settled it
It rises, because more people means more copying
why: Tempting, since 1,000 pooled clues really would reveal the truth. But copiers ignore their clues, so their choices add nothing, and the extra 990 people never get counted.
Right. By about 10 people a cascade has almost surely begun, and once it has, later choices carry no new clues. The paper's formulas give about 19% wrong at 75% accuracy, however long the line.
More people do copy, but copying doesn't change which way the cascade already points. The wrong-choice chance was fixed when the cascade began.

terms.means: A cascade in which everyone ends up copying the wrong choice
Pooling many people's clues so the group knows more than any one person

model.title: How often a line of people locks onto the right or wrong choice
model.note: Teaching model: this is the paper's binary-clue example (Section II.A). Both choices start equally likely, each clue points the right way with chance equal to the accuracy, an undecided person flips a coin, and people are counted in pairs. The curves are the paper's exact formulas (eqs. 1 and 3), with 'adopt' taken as the right choice; the opposite case is a mirror image. The model leaves out clues of different quality and any new public facts. The numbers come from these formulas, not from data on real people.

controls.label: Clue accuracy (chance a clue points the right way)
People who have chosen so far

steps.say: Picture a line of people choosing one after another, each with a private clue, just like before. Moving right along the bottom, the clues get more accurate.
The green curve is the chance the whole line ends up copying the right choice.
The orange curve is the chance it locks onto the wrong choice. The dashed curve is the chance nobody has started copying yet.
This slider moves the clue accuracy along the bottom.
And this one sets how many people have chosen so far. Watch the dashed curve sink.

explore.prompt: Play with both sliders. Look for where the orange curve stops caring about the line length, and how high it stays.

goals.text: Once copying has almost surely started, find the least accurate clue that still keeps the wrong lock-in point below the horizontal reference line.
hints: First make the line long enough that the dashed curve lies almost flat on the floor.
Then slide the clue accuracy up slowly and watch the orange point cross the horizontal reference line.
The crossing lies between 80% and 90% accuracy. You want the first step just past it.

goals.text: With clues barely better than a coin flip, find the shortest line after which fewer than 1 in 1,000 towns have still not started copying.
hints: Push the clue accuracy down to the weakest clues the slider allows.
Now add people two at a time and watch the 'No copying yet' number.
Each extra pair cuts that number to about a quarter. It drops below 0.1% somewhere between 6 and 14 people.

feedback.correct: Yes. A cascade usually starts within the first handful of people. After that, copiers' choices reveal nothing, so 990 more people cannot pull the town back to the right answer. The wrong-choice chance stays near the paper's figure for 75% accuracy.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to think more people means more evidence. But in a cascade, everyone after the first few ignores their own clue, so their choices carry no information. The chance of a wrong lock-in was set by those first few clues and hardly moves as the line grows.

steps.say: Start with clues right 60% of the time, and only two people so far. In 76% of towns those two choices already agree, so the next person copies whatever his clue says. Only the dashed 24% is still open.
Now let ten people choose. The dashed curve sinks to the floor. Each extra pair of people shrinks 'no copying yet' by the same factor, so it vanishes fast.
Look at the orange point. With 60% clues, about 37% of towns are all copying the wrong choice. It is locked in, because later choices add no new clues.

A cascade that locks onto the wrong choice is called a reverse cascade. Raise accuracy to 75%. The wrong chance drops to about 19%, and the right one rises to about 81%. That 81% is the paper's own figure.
Push to 90% clues. If ten people's clues were pooled, they would almost never be wrong. Yet the town still locks onto the wrong choice about 6 times in 100, not far from one person's 10.
Pooling everyone's clues is called information aggregation. A cascade blocks it: after the first few choices, everyone else's clues stay hidden in their heads.
So back at 75% clues with twenty people, the orange curve sits where it was at ten. A longer line doesn't rescue the town. Its fate was settled by its first few clues.

understand.explanation: Once two choices lean the same way, everyone after them copies, so a cascade usually starts within the first handful of people. The paper shows that the chance of no cascade shrinks exponentially: even with nearly useless clues, it is under 0.1% after only 10 people. Because so few clues decide the outcome, the town's choice is only about as reliable as those first clues. The paper's formulas give about an 81% chance of the right cascade when each clue is 75% accurate, so roughly 19% lock onto the wrong one. Adding people doesn't help, because copiers' choices reveal nothing about their own clues: the cascade blocks information aggregation. This is a stylised model with perfectly rational people and equally good clues. In a lab version using balls drawn from urns, cascades appeared in 41 of 56 runs, though real people do not always reason this neatly.
understand.quote: Even for very informative signals (where p is far from 1/2), the probability of the wrong cascade is remarkably high. The problem with cascades is that they prevent the aggregation of information of numerous individuals.

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation 3, for the case where adopting is right. Blue p is the clue accuracy slider, the paper's p. The purple power n/2 is the people slider: the paper counts people in pairs. The bracket [1 − (p − p²)^{n/2}] is one minus the dashed 'no copying yet' curve, which vanishes quickly. Once it has, the green result depends on p alone, and the wrong-cascade chance is what is left over.

concepts.recap: A cascade is decided by its first few clues, so even with good clues it locks onto the wrong choice surprisingly often, and a longer line doesn't fix that.

concepts.title: Too many copiers: the crowd can settle on either answer
concepts.idea: When voters copy the majority of a few earlier voters, raising the share of copiers past a tipping point turns one stable outcome (mostly right) into two (mostly right or mostly wrong).

predict.question: Now give the independent voters a real lean: their own clue points to the right answer 80% of the time instead of half. Compared with the even case you explored, what happens as you add more and more copiers?
options: The switch to two resting places comes sooner: fewer copiers are needed
The switch happens at exactly the same copier share as before
The switch comes later, but past it a mostly-wrong resting place still appears
There is no switch: with a lean, the vote always ends up mostly right
why: Tempting if you think any lean makes copying riskier. But the lean lifts the whole curve toward the right answer, so a low crossing needs a steeper S, and that takes more copiers, not fewer.
Tempting because the copiers' rule has not changed. But the resting places depend on the independent voters too. Their lean shifts the curve up, and that moves where the extra crossings first appear.

The lean lifts the curve, so the S must be steeper before it can dip back across the dashed line at the low end. In this model the switch moves from about 0.67 to about 0.85. Past it, a mostly-wrong resting place still sits beside the mostly-right one.

Tempting because the independent voters now push toward the truth. But with enough copiers the S gets steep enough to cross low anyway. A lean delays the split; it does not remove it. With every voter a copier, the independent voters have no say at all.

terms.means: A voter who copies: they pick whichever answer most of the earlier voters they look at chose (here, 2 or more out of 3)
A voter who ignores others and votes on their own clue, which picks the right answer with chance q
The share of herders at which one resting place splits into two; the paper writes it p_c
The state past the critical point: if you rerun the same vote many times, the final shares bunch at two different places

model.title: Where a long vote comes to rest
model.note: Teaching model: the paper's random-graph case. Each copier looks at exactly three earlier voters picked at random, treated as independent draws, as in the paper's own approximation. Only the long-run vote share over a very long line of voters is shown, not the random ups and downs of any single run. The curve and resting points come from the paper's equation (59). The slider settings are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How often own-clue voters pick right

x.label: Share voting for the right answer so far

y.label: Chance the next voter picks the right answer

series.label: Chance the next voter picks right

steps.say: Picture a long line of voters choosing between a right and a wrong answer. This curve says: if this share has voted right so far, how likely is the next voter to vote right?
The dashed line marks 'no change': there, the next vote matches the share so far.
Some voters simply copy. Each looks at three earlier voters, picked at random, and goes with whatever two or more of them chose. This slider sets how many voters are copiers.
Everyone else follows their own private clue. This slider sets how often that clue points to the right answer.
The dots and these numbers show where the vote ends up resting after very many voters.

explore.prompt: Hunt for the exact copier share where one resting place splits into two. Then see how lopsided the mistaken outcome can get.

goals.text: With independent voters split evenly, find the smallest copier share at which the vote can settle in two places (to within a couple of hundredths).
hints: Move the copier share slowly and watch the count of places the vote can settle.
In the walkthrough, 40% copiers gave one resting place and 80% gave two. The switch lies somewhere between.
Step by 0.01 between 0.6 and 0.7. Watch for the first moment the S-curve crosses the dashed line three times.

goals.text: Make the mistaken outcome extreme: if the vote goes wrong, no more than 1 voter in 10 should end up picking the right answer.
hints: Which slider pushes the two resting points apart?
More herders make the S steeper, so the outer crossings slide toward the edges. Keep an eye on the worst-case number.
You need to go well past the switch, somewhere in the 0.8s.

feedback.correct: Right. The independent voters' lean lifts the curve, so it takes a steeper S, meaning more herders, before a low crossing appears. In this model the switch moves from about 0.67 to about 0.85. Beyond that point, a mostly-wrong resting place still exists alongside the mostly-right one.
feedback.incorrect: The resting points are where the curve meets the dashed line, and both kinds of voter shape that curve. A lean toward the truth lifts it, which delays the split rather than causing it sooner or removing it. With enough herders, the S always gets steep enough to cross low.

steps.say: Start with no copiers at all. Everyone follows their own clue, and here those clues are coin tosses, so the curve is flat at one half. It meets the dashed line once: the vote settles at an even split.

Why is a crossing a resting place? Left of it, the curve is above the dashed line: the next vote is more likely right than the share so far, so the share creeps up. Right of it, the curve is below, so the share slips back.

Now make 40% of voters copiers. The paper calls them herders; a voter who follows their own clue is an independent voter. The curve bends into an S, because herders add weight to whichever answer is ahead. It still crosses only once.
Push herders to 80%. The S is now so steep that it crosses the dashed line three times.

The middle crossing is a knife-edge: above it the share keeps climbing, below it the share keeps falling. The outer crossings pull the vote in, so the crowd settles mostly right or mostly wrong, as the first chance votes tip it.

The herder share where one resting place splits into two is the critical point. Past it, the vote is in the two-peaks phase: rerun the same election many times and the results bunch at these two places.

understand.explanation: Herders go with the majority of three earlier voters picked at random, so they add weight to whichever answer is already ahead. Each independent voter follows only their own clue. With few herders, those clues dominate and the long vote has one resting place: an even split when the clues are coin tosses, mostly right when they lean toward the truth. Past a critical share of herders, the self-reinforcement is strong enough to create two resting places, one mostly right and one mostly wrong, and chance early votes decide which one the crowd lands in. As with the cascades you met earlier, the trouble comes from copying what others did rather than what they knew. Hisakado and Mori showed this by solving an equation for the long-run vote share, which has one solution below the critical point and three above it, and checked it with computer simulations; with only one or two voters looked at there is no such switch, and this is a model of idealised voters, not a measurement of real elections.
understand.quote: Below the critical point pc, we can obtain one solution Fig7 (a). We refer to this phase as the one-peak phase. In contrast, above the critical point, we obtain three solutions.
understand.quote_where: Appendix C (Mean field approximation and Stochastic differential equation)

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation (59). Z_∞ is the long-run share voting right (candidate C1). The left side is the dashed line and the right side is the curve, so resting points are where they meet. q is how often an independent voter picks right; p is the herder share. π(Z) is the chance that at least two of three random earlier voters chose right: 3Z² − 2Z³, a case of the paper's general sum. For q = 1/2 the paper finds p_c = 2/3.

concepts.recap: Herders reinforce whichever answer leads; past a critical share of herders, the same crowd can settle mostly right or mostly wrong, and early luck picks which.

concepts.title: Influencers change the pace, not the tipping point
concepts.idea: Making voters look at popular hubs rather than random earlier voters leaves the tipping point unchanged and only slows how quickly the vote settles.

predict.question: The paper also tried a 'fitness' network. There, some voters get extra pull, so a few grow into giant hubs that are even more dominant than the popular voters behind your switch. Copiers still follow the majority of three voters they look at. Compared with random copying, what does the paper find?
options: The tipping point drops: fewer copiers are needed before the crowd can lock onto the wrong answer
The tipping point stays where it was, and the vote still settles more slowly than with random copying
The tipping point stays, and settling speeds back up to full speed because everyone watches the same few voters
The crowd always ends on the right answer, because the giant voters are better informed
why: It feels natural that bigger influencers make a crowd easier to tip. But the paper's resting-point equation for the fitness network (36) is the same as the one for random copying, so the tipping point does not move.

Correct. The fitness network gives the same resting-point equation, so the tipping point is unchanged. The paper's simulations show no full-speed phase for it either: like the popular-voter network, it only slows settling.

Watching the same voters sounds like it should make people agree faster. In fact, reusing the same early votes again and again means old luck keeps echoing, so the wobble shrinks more slowly. The paper finds no full-speed phase with hubs.
Being popular here only means being looked at often. No voter in the model has a better clue, so hubs cannot steer the crowd toward the truth. They only change how long the tally keeps wobbling.

terms.means: A voter whom many later voters look at, like an influencer with a huge following
How fast the run-to-run wobble in the vote share dies away as more people vote (the 'settling speed' readout)
Settling at full speed: the wobble shrinks as fast as it would for independent coin flips
Settling more slowly than coin flips: early luck lingers in the tally for a long time

model.title: Where a long vote comes to rest, and how fast it gets there
model.note: Teaching model: the paper's mean-field results for copiers who each look at three earlier voters (r = 3) and follow their majority. The switch chooses between two cases. When it is off, copiers look at random earlier voters (the paper's random graph). When it is on, copiers pick earlier voters in proportion to how many links they already have (the paper's Barabási–Albert network). The curve and resting points come from equations (59), (12) and (30), which are identical for both cases. Settling speed is 2 − 2L, capped at 100%, following Appendix B, with L taken from equations (15) and (33). Where there are two resting places, the readout uses the slower one. The mean-field approach treats the three looked-at voters as independent draws and ignores finite-run effects, which the paper's simulations show can be large. Slider settings are illustrative, not the paper's data.

x.label: Share voting for the right answer so far

y.label: Chance the next voter picks the right answer

steps.say: This is the same picture as before. The solid curve gives the chance that the next voter picks right. Where it crosses the dashed line, the vote comes to rest.
Here is the one new switch. When it is off, copiers look at three random earlier voters. When it is on, they look at popular voters, the ones others have already looked at most.
Here is the new readout, settling speed. At 100%, the tally's wobble from run to run dies away as fast as it would for coin flips. Lower means early luck lingers longer.

explore.prompt: Flip the switch at different shares of copiers and different clue qualities. Keep one eye on the curve and the 'places to settle' box, and the other on the settling speed.

goals.text: With copiers looking at random earlier voters, find a crowd that has two possible resting places yet still settles at full speed.
hints: Copiers slow things down most when the three voters they look at often disagree. Where would they rarely disagree?
Beyond the tipping point, each resting place sits where almost everyone agrees. So copiers deep in that region are hardly ever torn.
Leave the switch off and push the share of copiers well past the tipping point, toward the far right of the slider.

goals.text: Make own-clue voters right 70% of the time. Then, with copiers looking at popular voters, give the crowd two possible resting places using as few copiers as you can (stay below 85%).
hints: Watch the 'Places the vote can settle' box while you raise the share of copiers.
Better own clues make the crowd harder to tip, so expect the tipping point higher than it was with coin-flip clues.
It lies between 80% and 85%. Once you find it, flip the switch off and on there to check whether it moves.

feedback.correct: Right. The paper's fitness network gives the same resting-point equation as random copying, so the tipping point stays put. Its giant hubs, like the popular voters behind the switch, only slow how fast the tally settles.
feedback.incorrect: You probably expected bigger influencers to change where the crowd ends up, or to make it agree faster. In the paper's model, hubs leave the resting points and the tipping point untouched. Because they keep reusing the same early votes, they only make the wobble die out more slowly.

steps.say: Start with random copying and 30% copiers. There is one resting place, and settling speed is 100%. This full-speed settling is called normal diffusion.
Now flip the switch so copiers look at popular voters. A voter whom many others look at is called a hub. Watch the curve and the resting point: neither moves.

Only settling speed changed, to 55%. Hubs get re-read again and again, so early luck lingers. The paper calls this pace the convergence speed; settling slower than coin flips is called super diffusion.
Push copiers to 66%, just short of the tipping point you met before, with the switch off. Even random copying nearly stalls here, at about 2%.
Step to 70%. A second resting point appears, so the vote can settle in two places. That is the two-peaks phase.
Flip to popular voters at the same 70%. Still two places, at exactly the same spots. The tipping point is the same with or without hubs.
Last stop: 75% copiers. Both networks settle in the same two places, but hubs settle at 25% speed against 50% for random copying. Same destinations, slower journey.

understand.explanation: Switching copiers from random earlier voters to popular ones left the curve and its resting points exactly where they were, so the tipping point did not move. What changed was the pace. With hubs, the tally always settles more slowly than coin flips once anyone copies. Random copying, by contrast, reaches full speed both well below and well above the tipping point. The paper derived the long-run equations for a random network and for a popular-voter (Barabási–Albert) network. The resting-point equations came out identical (equations 12 and 30), and only the speed condition differed (15 versus 33). A 'fitness' network with even stronger hubs gave the same tipping point. Simulations of 32,000-voter runs agreed, although the authors note large finite-run effects and cannot rule out a full-speed phase in every setting (for example, when copiers look at nine voters). Their conclusion holds only within this simple majority-copying model: hubs change how much the vote wobbles, not where it ends.
understand.quote: In conclusion, the inﬂuence of hubs can only be seen in the convergence speed and cannot be seen in the phase transition between the one-peak and two-peaks phases.

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation (33) for three looked-at voters. L is how strongly copiers pull the tally toward its own past, p is the share of copiers, and m = 2 × (share voting right) − 1 at a resting point. For random copying (equation 15) the '½[1 + …]' is missing, so L can fall below ½ and speed can reach 100%. With hubs, L never drops below ½, so full speed is impossible once anyone copies. Speed = 2 − 2L comes from Appendix B: variance shrinks like τ^{2L−2}.

concepts.recap: Hubs leave the crowd's possible endings and its tipping point unchanged; they only make the vote take longer to settle.

concepts.title: A crowd of millions, toppled by one small fact
concepts.idea: Since a cascade rests only on the few clues before it started, its size adds no evidence, so one public clue weaker than a single private clue can make people use their own information again and reverse it.

predict.question: A new restaurant has a long queue. The first two diners chose it, and 200 people have since joined only because they saw the queue. Then a critic posts a mildly negative review, about half as convincing as a diner's own glance at the menu. In the model, what does the next arrival do?
options: Goes with their own impression: joins if the menu looks good, walks away if it doesn't
Joins anyway, because 200 people outweigh one mild review
Walks away no matter what, because the review sends everyone home
It depends on whether the queue holds 200 or 2,000 people
why: Right. The queue rests on about 1.3 clues' worth of evidence. Half a clue against it drops the lean below one clue, so the arrival's own impression now tips the decision.
It feels as if 200 people are 200 votes. But they all copied without using their own clues, so together they add no evidence. Only the first two diners count.
Half a clue is far too weak to decide on its own. It only cancels part of the evidence for joining, so an arrival who likes the menu still joins.
Size is exactly what doesn't matter. Copiers reveal nothing, so 200 or 2,000 followers leave the evidence, and the effect of the review, unchanged.

terms.means: A clue everyone can see at the same time, such as a published study or an official report
How much real evidence a cascade rests on. It does not grow as more people copy
Easily broken: a small amount of new information can end the cascade

model.title: What holds a copying crowd up, counted in private clues
model.note: Teaching model of the paper's binary case (Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch, Sections II.A and III.A). There are two equally likely states, every private clue has the same accuracy, people reason as perfect Bayesians, and the crowd is in an adopt cascade started by two adopts. Ties are broken by a coin flip, as in the paper. Evidence is measured in units of one private clue (log-odds). The shared clue always points against adopting, and you set its strength freely. Accuracy, crowd size and clue strength are illustrative settings, not the paper's data.

Next person's belief that adopting is right, if their own clue says no
Next person's belief that adopting is right, if their own clue says yes

steps.say: Picture a crowd where everyone is copying and adopting. Each bar measures a reason for or against adopting, counted in private clues.
These two bars are what the first two people's choices reveal.
This slider sets how often one private clue is right. It changes how much the second choice is worth.

explore.prompt: Pile on copiers, then find out how small a shared clue can be and still get the next person to trust their own clue again.

goals.text: With at least half a million people copying, make the next person's own clue decide again, using a shared clue less than half as strong as one private clue
hints: Copiers add nothing, so the size of the crowd won't help or hurt you. What else is on the 'for' side?
The shared clue doesn't have to beat the crowd. It only has to cancel the smaller of the two chooser bars.
Raise the shared clue one step at a time and watch 'Own clue decides'. It flips just after the shared clue bar grows taller than the second chooser's bar.

feedback.correct: Yes. The queue's evidence is set by the first two diners, about 1.3 clues. A review worth half a clue pulls the lean below one clue, so the next arrival's own impression decides. The 200 copiers never entered the calculation.
feedback.incorrect: The pull of a big crowd is strong, but in this model copiers reveal nothing: each ignored their own clue. The queue rests on about 1.3 clues, so half a clue against it is enough for the arrival's own impression to decide again. That impression can point either way.

steps.say: Here is a crowd in an adopt cascade. The first chooser followed their own clue, so their choice reveals exactly one private clue.
The second chooser's adopt is weaker evidence. On a yes clue they adopt, but on a no clue they were tied and flipped a coin. So their choice counts for only about a third of a clue.

Now add a million copiers. Their bar stays at zero, and the total stays at 1.32 clues. Copiers ignored their own clues, so their choices reveal nothing. The paper calls this total the depth of a cascade, and it does not grow with the crowd.
With a lean of 1.32 clues, even someone whose own clue says no still leans yes, at 57%. So they copy, and their own clue doesn't decide.
Now publish a report everyone sees: public information against adopting, worth a fifth of one private clue. The lean drops to 1.12 clues. That is still above one, so people still copy.
At 0.3 of a clue the lean is 1.02, just above one. The next person still copies.

At 0.35 the report has just outweighed the second chooser's choice. The lean falls below one clue. A no clue now tips the next person to reject (belief 49%), and a yes clue still means adopt. Their own clue decides again.

The twist: a million followers rested on about 1.3 private clues, and a fact a third as strong as one hunch knocked them loose. Choices carry information again, so the crowd can turn. This is why the paper calls cascades fragile.

understand.explanation: A cascade's evidence is fixed the moment it starts. The first chooser's choice reveals one private clue. The second chooser's adopt is weaker, because they might have adopted on a no clue plus a coin flip. Everyone after ignored their own clue, so a million copiers add nothing. A public clue therefore only has to cancel the second chooser's choice, worth well under one private clue here, for the next person's own clue to decide again. Once people act on their own clues, their choices carry information and the crowd can swing the other way. The paper proves this for its simple binary model (Result 3) and offers hybrid corn and the oat bran fad as possible illustrations, not tests. The model assumes identical, perfectly rational people and leaves out copying driven by social pressure.
understand.quote: Intuitively, cascades aggregate the information of only a few early individuals' actions. The public information thus needs only to offset the information conveyed by the action of the last individual before the start of the cascade, even if millions subsequently imitated.

check.task: Show that a huge crowd is no harder to topple. With private clues right at least 90% of the time and at least half a million copiers, make the next person's own clue decide, using a shared clue less than a third as strong as one private clue.
check.hint: The copiers add nothing, so set them as high as you like. With sharper clues, check how tall the second chooser's bar is: that is all the shared clue must cancel.
check.misconception: A bigger crowd holds more evidence, so it takes a stronger fact to sway it.

(1 + s₂) is the cascade's evidence: one clue from the first chooser plus s₂ from the second, whose adopt may hide a coin flip. concepts.recap: A cascade's size adds no evidence. It rests on the first few choices, so a public fact weaker than one person's hunch can make people think for themselves again and turn the crowd.
